comment: The timber frame is part of the building too. Makes sense to recognise more than what you can see from the sidewalk.
Fine with protecting the architecture. I don't have much of an opinion on adding another former owner to the history.
I work nearby. A clearer account of the old furniture business seems worth keeping with the building record.
Historic structure deserves attention alongside the facade. The post and beam construction is the strongest part of this amendment for me.
Recording the business history is fine. I am less comfortable extending the protected attributes inside the building without understanding what that means for routine work.
nice building. the architecture part gets my vote
I pass this corner, but I would need to read more before deciding which interior features should be protected.
The history does not bother me. I worry about making future repairs more complicated; I cannot tell from this notice what approvals would be involved.
Documenting a long-running local business has value even if I have no strong view about the structural designation.
Yes please. I like knowing why an ordinary-looking commercial building matters, rather than just seeing a heritage label.
The historical addition reads reasonably. I do not know enough about timber structures to judge the second part.
Another round of heritage paperwork for one building? I would rather the City spend its attention elsewhere. Against expanding this.
I work in a small music venue. Licensing it according to what it actually does seems much easier to explain than putting everything in the nightclub bucket.
Smaller spaces should have a sensible licence category. I still care about noise from the premises near my home; those are both reasonable things to care about.
Under 151 people can still feel like a lot next door. I favour clearer zoning and licensing alignment, but this cutoff does not persuade me.
more room for small venues to exist, yes. I like the direction of this
The under-151 definition helps me understand the licensing side. Too early to rate the potential zoning changes from a direction to assess and consult.
Mostly interested in the two departments using rules that fit together. I do not have a strong view on the exact occupant-load threshold.
Does the proposed category reflect how a venue runs on a busy evening? I would like that explained. Getting zoning and licensing to line up sounds worthwhile.
I operate a small venue and would prefer a definition based on activities alone. A sharp size cutoff seems awkward even though I support aligning the rules.
I go out sometimes but the licence categories are new to me. No strong position yet.
I travel home after evening shifts. Support the smaller-venue change; no particular opinion on the planning work.
Honestly I would prefer fewer places to dance near homes, full stop. Even a small one. This proposal is not for me.
A city needs places for smaller shows and nights out. This looks like a useful licensing distinction, with further work needed on the zoning side.
The name of the licence matters less to me than knowing which category an actual business will land in. I need examples before voting yes or no.
I enjoy small venues but I don't see why occupant load should decide this. Neutral on the alignment work.
Seems fair. I am reading this as a different licence based on operations, not a free pass on every other rule.
please make the licensing and zoning explanations agree. The threshold itself is not my main issue.
I work in second-hand retail. Flexible hours and a register in an approved format sound useful. I cannot speak for the nightclub definition.
I am fine with updating the register format and dropping videotape-store licensing. Removing the specified operating-hour restrictions is the part that leaves me against the package.
Still keeping a register, just not necessarily an ink book, seems sensible. Broadly in favour of this tidy-up.
The record-format change makes sense to me. Not bothered either way about the specified hours, and I support retiring the videotape chapter.
I run an entertainment space. The three-of-four test still seems hard to apply to different sorts of events. I like the other housekeeping changes.
Approved electronic records seem perfectly reasonable. I also prefer having the nightclub criteria written out clearly.
videotape-store licence repeal, sure. The rest needs more reading than I have done
Changing the book format is one thing; removing routine submissions of register information is another. I am uneasy about bundling those together and have not settled on the whole proposal.
The hours flexibility and clearer entertainment definition appeal to me. Neutral on how shops maintain their goods registers.
I prefer retaining the existing restrictions and routine register submissions. I am not persuaded by the entertainment definition either. No view on the videotape chapter.
The ink-book requirement feels dated. Let an approved format do the same job. I have no strong view on the nightclub part.
Mostly outside my experience. Repealing the videotape-store licence sounds fine; skipping judgement on the other bits for now.
A fairly practical update. I would still like a plain-language example of which entertainment businesses meet three of the four criteria.
I favour keeping the specified shop hours. The videotape repeal is fine, but I don't support the package overall.

I sell refreshments and like opening up applications and having longer on-block hours. The new on-foot licence requirements look like a lot for a very small operation. Still unsure about the broader permit regime.
A food option on the way home is welcome. Longer vending hours sound useful, and visible licensing makes sense to me.
More applications are fine in principle. Twelve hours on one block is the bit I disagree with. I need more detail on the new permit setup.
yes to more food choices! neutral on the permit overhaul, that is not something i know much about
I work in a storefront and worry about space for customers and deliveries. Not against every vendor, but I do not favour more applications and longer stays as proposed.
I like street food and support new applications. Keeping a clear route along the sidewalk matters to me too. I am neutral about the longer hours.
Lifting the specified application moratoriums and updating the permit system seems a useful direction. Unsure whether the on-foot insurance requirement is proportionate.
As a food-service worker I like seeing a clearer path for vending businesses. Happy with the hours change and the licensing requirements.
I am often walking between connections. The twelve-hour stay worries me where space is tight; I cannot judge the new regime from the short description.
No thanks. I want my block quiet and empty when I get home, and I am not interested in another place to buy a snack. Unsure about the on-foot licence.
I enjoy buying from vendors. The new licence and insurance package for someone selling on foot feels heavy, though. Mixed on the proposal as a whole.
I work at a shop and I think nearby vendors can add to the street. Supportive of the package, with practical questions about where everyone fits.
I favour accepting applications and a new permit framework. Requiring the whole on-foot licence package is my sticking point, so I oppose this version.
Health checks and a visible licence sound reasonable. I have not decided on the space and hours questions.
longer hours would suit when I travel. no real opinion on the new regime and not sure about the on-foot part
I like a quick food stop but twelve hours in the same block sounds too long to me. The licensing part seems reasonable.
I rent an apartment. Recovering the cost of reissuing a sign seems reasonable, and I support the listed social-housing exemptions.
I would rather the sign reissue cost be covered through the program. I support the social-housing waiver but do not favour this fee package overall.
I work in building operations. Defined charges are easier to plan around than uncertainty. In favour of these changes, including the targeted sign-fee exemptions.
The remedial-work fees are the strongest part for me. I support recovering those costs rather than leaving them entirely with the general budget.
Fine with waiving the sign fee for the listed social-housing providers. Less sure how the other charges fit into the rest of RentSafeTO.
A charge just to reissue a sign feels fussy to me. The exemption and remedial-work changes still make the overall proposal worth supporting.
I help manage rental properties and disagree with the new sign charge and remedial-work fee approach. Neutral on the exemption.
yes. clear signs matter and so does having a way to recover remedial costs
The specified social-housing waiver seems fair. I have no strong view on the sign charge and need more context on remedial costs.
I work in social housing. Glad the sign reissue waiver is specified for eligible providers. I support the other fee changes too; this is not an exemption from every fee.
Every problem gets another fee attached. I do not support this package, exemptions included. I would prefer a different funding approach.
Support charging for sign reissues and remedial work. I disagree with exempting some providers from the sign charge, enough that I oppose the package.
Neutral on the forty-something-dollar sign fee. More interested in the remedial-work part and keeping the specified exemption.
I visit family in an apartment building but have never dealt with this program. Not enough background to pick a side.
I rent too, though I mainly follow city issues through my commute. Support the listed waiver; no strong opinion on the other two charges.
Reasonable on paper. As a tenant, the outcome I care about is maintenance actually being done; these fees alone do not tell me how that will go.
I use permit parking. Being able to find the excluded addresses in one schedule sounds helpful, and I favour clarifying who has authority.
The address list part is easy to understand. I cannot follow the change to Community Council authority well enough to rate it yet.
I work on housing applications. A clear decision route and one consolidated address schedule would make the process easier to explain.
One list sounds good. I do not have a strong view about which council body handles these decisions.
I prefer keeping more of these decisions with Community Council. A consolidated schedule is still a good idea.
Clearer responsibility is worthwhile even on an unglamorous parking procedure. Support both parts.
I do trades work and check parking eligibility when arranging visits. A single list would help me; unsure about the authority wording.
As someone looking at rentals, I want to check an address before moving. Support the schedule, still unsure about the council procedure bit.
I would prefer the existing arrangements over this procedural change. Consolidating the exclusions does not win me over either.
I visit friends in permit areas. Need a plainer explanation of how this changes an individual address decision.
one place to check an address, please. no opinion on who gets the decision
I want every parking decision near me argued out locally, however long it takes. Keep that part as it is. The combined address list is fine.
